summary: Flags unnecessary square-bracket notation for static property names where dot notation is valid.
fixDescription: Replaces obj["property"] with obj.property when the property name is a valid identifier and not a reserved word (unless allowKeywords is false).
hazards: Rewriting obj["prop"] to obj.prop fails if prop is not a valid identifier (e.g., contains hyphen) as it becomes invalid syntax.
If the property name matches a reserved word (e.g., "class") and allowKeywords is false, the fix incorrectly applies dot notation causing a parse error.
When the property name is a numeric literal string (e.g., "123"), dot notation (obj.123) is invalid syntax and the fix breaks parsing.
If the object expression has side effects (e.g., obj()["prop"]), extracting it for dot notation may alter evaluation order or cause errors if obj() is not callable.
In strict mode, if the property name is "eval" or "arguments", dot notation may trigger different behavior due to language restrictions on those identifiers.
Comments attached to the brackets or quotes are lost during the rewrite as the autofix replaces the entire member expression token.
If the property name is a Unicode escape sequence (e.g., "\u0061") that resolves to an identifier, the fix may produce obj.a but the original was intentionally obfuscated or encoded.
When used with optional chaining (obj?.["prop"]), the fix incorrectly produces obj?.prop which changes nullish behavior if obj is null/undefined.
In class fields with private names (e.g., obj["#private"]), dot notation is invalid and the fix breaks encapsulation or causes syntax errors.
If the property name is a getter/setter accessor, dot notation may invoke it differently in edge cases involving inheritance or proxy objects.

The fix may break code relying on bracket notation to access properties via variables that coincidentally match a string literal (e.g., var prop = "foo"; obj[prop] vs obj["foo"] after variable removal).
When the object is a super call (super["prop"]), rewriting to super.prop is invalid syntax as super only supports dot notation in specific contexts, but the fix may misapply.
